title: Character Analysis
description: Detailed analysis of Enid, Del, Viv, Mai and Brod — methods, motivations and dramatic functions.
content_html:
Enid Matthews

Enid is the play's central character — the person whose choices, fears and history drive the action. She is a first-generation Jamaican immigrant who came to England around 1959 as part of the Windrush generation. She works as a hospital cleaner — sometimes at two jobs simultaneously — and has devoted her life to her daughters' security. Enid's defining strategy is assimilation: she speaks 'proper' English, dismisses Obeah as superstition, and suppresses any reference to Jamaican culture that might mark her daughters as outsiders.

Enid's backstory is gradually revealed across the play. She was abandoned by her husband after he subjected her to domestic violence — cruelty rooted in the racism and humiliation he suffered at work. Brod discloses this to Del in Scene 7. Enid's mother called her 'Miss English' and the two became estranged; Enid sent money home but kept emotional distance. When her mother dies in Scene 3, Enid's grief is compounded by the estrangement that can never now be resolved. Her controlling behaviour is not cruelty — it is a survivor's response to racism, poverty, abuse and loss.

Key Fact

Enid's controlling behaviour has three roots: (1) her abusive marriage — she will not allow her daughters to experience what she endured; (2) her mother's death and their estranged relationship — she cannot bear to lose her daughters the same way; (3) her experience of racism as a Windrush immigrant — she believes assimilation is the only protection she can offer. Understanding these three drivers is essential for top-band analysis.

Del (Delores)

Del is the elder daughter, aged 18. She is the play's most instinctive character — rebellious, sensory, drawn to things she cannot fully articulate. She stays out late, loses her job after arguing with her manager, and initially refuses to have her palm read by Mai. But she is drawn irresistibly to Mai's world. She later discovers she is dyslexic, which reframes her educational struggles: she was not lazy but struggling with an undiagnosed barrier. She becomes pregnant — the father absent — and eventually moves into Mai's Deptford bedsit, beginning her training as Mai's spiritual successor.

By the final scene, Del has been transformed. She reads Enid's palm — a spiritual act she once refused — and in doing so offers Enid the bridge to her own heritage that Enid could never build alone. Del's arc is about discovering her true identity: not the respectable English daughter Enid wanted, and not simply a rebellious teenager, but someone with a genuine gift and a genuine heritage to inhabit.

Viv is the younger daughter, aged 17. She appears to be Enid's success story: educated, articulate, preparing for A-level exams. She has adopted English culture more fully than Del and seems comfortable in it. But Pinnock complicates this apparent conformity through Viv's educational rebellion. She walks out of one of her exams — an act of defiance against a Eurocentric curriculum that, she says, has no place for her. She feels invisible within it: 'no matter how hard I search for myself in them books, I'm never there.' She plans to study Black Studies at university — a subject that acknowledges her existence — and the play ends with her leaving for precisely that future.

Viv's rebellion is intellectual rather than physical. Her crisis is not a pregnancy or a departure from home but a crisis of educational identity — a recognition that the path Enid mapped for her was built on a curriculum that erased her. Both daughters ultimately reject Enid's assimilation strategy, but they do so in ways that reflect their different personalities.

Mai

Mai is an Obeah woman who lives in a Deptford bedsit. She is physically declining throughout the play — nearly fainting at one point, clearly dying by the end — but her spiritual authority is undiminished. She has an estranged adult son. She charges no fee for Enid's final reading, out of sympathy. Pinnock presents Mai not as superstition to be overcome but as a figure of genuine wisdom and cultural continuity. She sees clearly what each character needs: Del needs to be recognised as a healer; Enid needs permission to reconnect with what she suppressed. Mai does not impose — she offers.

Brod is Enid's childhood friend from Jamaica, a fellow Windrush immigrant. He appears on stage in Scenes 2, 3 and 7 — he is not an absent or offstage character. He has a serious drinking problem, has children he no longer sees, and is deeply disenchanted with life in England. He describes a friend, Gullyman, who achieved financial success but still suffered a breakdown — arguing that England's racism corrodes everyone eventually, however successful they appear.

Brod's most important dramatic function is in Scene 7, when he tells Del about her father's abusive treatment of Enid and about the racism that drove it. He is the only character who can deliver this truth — not because he is wise, but because he was there. Pinnock uses Brod to show that the truth about the past must eventually be spoken, even if imperfectly, by imperfect people.

Key Fact

Understanding the playwright's specific choices — structure, language, staging and context — is essential for top-band analysis. Make sure you can discuss how form and content work together to create meaning for the audience.

Effective drama analysis requires attention to stagecraft — considering not just what happens but how the playwright shapes the audience's response through every element of performance and text. In your exam response, identify specific techniques and explain their effect precisely.

practice_questions.text: How does Pinnock present Enid as a character in Leave Taking? [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Multi-layered analysis. Discusses: Enid's assimilation strategy, its roots in racism/abuse/estrangement from her mother, her emotional collapse after her mother's death, her gradual movement towards acceptance in the final scene. Analyses Pinnock's dramatic methods — Enid's dialogue, her relationship with each character, the revelation of her backstory via Brod. Links to Windrush context.

Mid band (9–16): Clear analysis with evidence across the play.

Lower band (1–8): Describes Enid without analysing Pinnock's methods.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Pinnock and the unseen writer present a mother whose relationship with her children is defined by sacrifice. Consider language, form and structure. [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Perceptive comparison. Analyses Pinnock's Enid — sacrificing cultural identity, language, emotional authenticity to protect daughters from racism. Compares with unseen writer's methods. AO3 integrated.

Mid band (9–16): Clear comparison.

Lower band (1–8): Limited comparison.

practice_questions.text: How does Pinnock present Del's transformation as a character across Leave Taking? [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Traces Del's arc from rebellious elder daughter (refusing Mai's reading in Scene 1) to Mai's trained spiritual successor (performing the reading in Scene 8). Discusses: dyslexia diagnosis, pregnancy, move to Mai's bedsit, the candle symbolism. Links to themes of cultural belonging and identity reclamation.

Mid band (9–16): Clear analysis with evidence.

Lower band (1–8): Basic description.

practice_questions.text: Explore how Pinnock presents Viv's rebellion against the education system in Leave Taking. [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Analyses Viv's rebellion as intellectual and cultural. Discusses: the exam walkout, her statement about invisibility in the curriculum, her choice of Black Studies. Contrasts with Del's different form of rebellion. Links to second-generation immigrant experience and the exclusion of Caribbean culture from mainstream education.

Mid band (9–16): Clear analysis with evidence.

Lower band (1–8): Basic description.

practice_questions.text: How does Pinnock use the character of Mai to present Caribbean cultural values? [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Analyses Mai as the play's representative of authentic Caribbean spiritual tradition. Discusses: Obeah as legitimate wisdom; Mai's insight into each character's needs; the passing of her notebook to Del; her contrast with Enid's dismissal of the past. Links to Pinnock's argument about the value of what assimilation suppresses.

Mid band (9–16): Clear analysis.

Lower band (1–8): Basic description.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Pinnock and the unseen writer present a character who holds a truth the family needs to hear. Consider language, form and structure. [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Perceptive comparison. Analyses Pinnock's Brod in Scene 7 — imperfect, drunk, disenchanted, but the only character who can tell Del about her father. His function as reluctant truth-teller. Compares with the unseen writer's methods. AO3 integrated.

Mid band (9–16): Clear comparison.

Lower band (1–8): Limited comparison.

knowledge_checks.q: Del is the _____ daughter in Leave Taking, aged 18.
What does Viv plan to study at university at the end of the play?
Enid's controlling behaviour has three roots: her abusive marriage, her mother's death and estrangement, and her experience of _____.
In which scenes does Brod appear on stage?
Match each character to their key dramatic function:
right: First-generation immigrant whose suppression of heritage drives the play's conflict
Elder daughter (18) who becomes Mai's spiritual successor and offers reconciliation
Obeah woman who facilitates healing without imposing — passes her role to Del
Windrush friend who delivers the truth about the abusive marriage in Scene 7

flashcard_questions.q: What are the three roots of Enid's controlling behaviour?
flashcard_questions.a: Her abusive marriage; her estranged relationship with her mother and the mother's death; her experience of racism as a Windrush immigrant.

flashcard_questions.q: Del is described as the _____ daughter, aged ___.
Viv is described as the _____ daughter, aged ___.
What disability does Del discover she has, and why does it matter?
flashcard_questions.a: Dyslexia — it reframes her school struggles as undiagnosed difficulty, not laziness or rebellion.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Enid's mother call her, and what does it reveal?
flashcard_questions.a: 'Miss English' — revealing Enid's mother mocked her assimilation and the two were estranged.

flashcard_questions.q: What form does Viv's rebellion take?
flashcard_questions.a: Walking out of an A-level exam and choosing to study Black Studies — a rejection of Eurocentric education, not a physical or romantic crisis.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does Mai charge no fee for Enid's final reading?
flashcard_questions.a: Out of sympathy — she recognises Enid's suffering and offers her gift freely.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Brod reveal in Scene 7, and why is he the one to do it?
flashcard_questions.a: That Enid's husband was abusive, driven by workplace racism. Brod is the only person who was there and can tell the truth.

flashcard_questions.q: Who is Gullyman, and why does Brod mention him?
flashcard_questions.a: A friend who achieved financial success but still suffered a breakdown — evidence that England's racism corrodes everyone eventually.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Del's arc in one sentence?
flashcard_questions.a: From rebellious elder daughter refusing Mai's reading (Scene 1) to Mai's spiritual successor performing the reading for Enid (Scene 8).

glossary_terms.definition: Caribbean immigrants who came to Britain between 1948 and 1971 — Enid, Brod, and their friends are all from this generation.
Adopting the norms of the dominant culture at the expense of one's own heritage — Enid's survival strategy.
A learning difference affecting reading and writing — Del's diagnosis reframes her school struggles as unrecognised difficulty.
Emotional or physical distance between people once close — Enid's relationship with her Jamaican mother.
The loss of ideals and hope — Brod's defining characteristic as a Windrush immigrant.
The passing on of spiritual knowledge and practice — Mai bequeaths her Obeah role to Del.
The playwright's use of dramatic techniques including staging, lighting, dialogue, and structure to create meaning.

exam_tip_html: When writing about Character Analysis, focus your analysis on the specific dramatic and structural choices the playwright makes. Examiners reward responses that connect language details to wider themes, and that show understanding of the social and historical context in which the play was written. Avoid retelling the plot — instead, explain the effect of specific techniques on the audience.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • This lesson has covered the key ideas and dramatic techniques relevant to Character Analysis. Make sure you can discuss specific examples from the text, link techniques to themes, and embed relevant context in your analysis.
